neighbors.heading: a restless heart
neighbors.text: Today a few Meccans looked at the idols and kept looking for the God of Ibrahim. Catholics treasure a seeker's prayer too. Saint Augustine, after years of searching, opened his Confessions to God with: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The Church teaches that the longing for God is written in the human heart.
neighbors.difference: The hanifs turned toward the one God of Ibrahim before any revelation came to them. Augustine found his rest in Christ and his Church, and Catholics read an honest search as already drawn by grace.
neighbors.shared: the search itself can be a way of turning toward home.
neighbors.sources: Augustine, Confessions I.1 (Pusey 1838) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 27 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the noble search
neighbors.text: Today Zayd ibn Amr walked away from what everyone around him did, and kept asking. Buddhists remember a search like it. Before his awakening, the Buddha told of studying with two respected teachers, mastering what they taught, and leaving each one because it wasn't yet the answer. He called it the noble search: looking for what doesn't age, sicken or die.
neighbors.difference: The hanifs were looking for the one God of Ibrahim, the Lord of the House. The Buddha's search wasn't for a creator; it was for freedom from suffering, which he taught is found by seeing clearly.
neighbors.shared: it takes courage to keep asking when everyone else has stopped.

neighbors.heading: don't stand by
neighbors.text: Today the young Prophet stood with men who swore to side with anyone wronged in Mecca, even a stranger. The Torah gives Jews the same duty in one line: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." The rabbis read it broadly: if you see someone drowning, or robbed, and you can help, you must.
neighbors.difference: The league was a pact clans chose to make, and the Prophet later said he'd still answer its call. For Jews the duty is a command from God at Sinai, binding on each person whether or not anyone else signs on.
neighbors.shared: a stranger with no one should still find someone on their side.

neighbors.heading: decide before the moment
neighbors.text: Today a group promised in advance to stand with anyone wronged. Psychologists found why that matters. In experiments by Bibb Latané and John Darley, people alone helped someone in trouble far more often than people in a group, where each one waited for someone else. A promise made ahead of time may help break that waiting.
neighbors.difference: The league was sworn in a house in Mecca, and the Prophet later tied it to a call from God to stand for justice. The psychology describes how people act; it doesn't say who calls us to act.
neighbors.shared: someone has to go first; you can decide now it'll be you.
neighbors.sources: Darley and Latané, "Bystander intervention in emergencies," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: truthful living
neighbors.text: Today Mecca called him al-Amin, the trustworthy, a man whose word matched what happened. Sikhs hold the same ideal high. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says truth is above everything, and higher still is truthful living. For Sikhs, being honest isn't only what you say; it's how you earn, trade and treat people every day.
neighbors.difference: Mecca's name for him was praise from his neighbors, even his opponents, before the message came. For Sikhs, truthful living is the path itself, part of remembering God, who in the Mool Mantar is named as Truth.
neighbors.shared: the people who know you best can say: your word holds.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: speak the truth
neighbors.text: Today he was known as al-Sadiq, the truthful, long before he made any claim. Hindus have a teacher's farewell to students that starts the same way. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, the teacher's first words of advice to those leaving his school are: speak the truth, practice dharma. Another Upanishad says truth alone wins, words India later put on its national emblem.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, the Prophet's truthfulness was the ground people stood on when he spoke of God. In the Upanishads, satya, truth, is also woven into the order of the world itself, dharma, which a life is meant to keep.
neighbors.shared: a life that tells the truth becomes a voice people trust.

neighbors.heading: the quiet place first
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet went up to Hira for nights alone, with Khadijah keeping him in food. Buddhists remember a seat like his cave. Before his awakening, the Buddha went to a quiet grove beside a river and sat down to strive, and later he sent his monks to the forest, to the roots of trees, to sit.
neighbors.difference: At Hira the Prophet worshiped in the way of Ibrahim, and the angel came to him there. The Buddha sat in meditation, not prayer to a God, and awakening came from seeing the mind clearly.
neighbors.shared: some things can only be heard once the noise goes quiet.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 26, Ariyapariyesana Sutta (paraphrase) · Majjhima Nikaya 19 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: up the mountain to pray
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet climbed to a cave and came back, again and again. Christians know that rhythm from Jesus. Luke says: "he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God." Mark adds: "rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed."
neighbors.difference: Muslims honor the Prophet as a human messenger seeking God before revelation came to him. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God, praying to his Father in a closeness they understand as unique to him.
neighbors.shared: the people who carried the most went off alone to pray first.

items.lessonTitle: The sun in my right hand

neighbors.heading: not for sale
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet said that even the sun in one hand and the moon in the other couldn't buy his message. Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote about that kind of refusal in his essay Self-Reliance: "Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind." For Emerson, what you hold true isn't something to trade for comfort or approval.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet refused because the message was from God, not his to give away. Emerson places the last word in a person's own honest mind, and the essay leans on no scripture.
neighbors.shared: some things aren't for sale, and saying no can still cost tears.

neighbors.heading: the whole world
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet turned down an offer as big as the sky. Catholics hear Jesus ask a question close to it: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?" Catholics also remember Saint Thomas More, who kept his conscience even when the king's favor and his life were the price.
neighbors.difference: In the sirah, the Prophet is refusing to give up the message God gave him to deliver. Jesus speaks of every disciple's own soul, and Catholics hear it as the cost of following him.
neighbors.shared: what's worth everything can't be traded for anything.

neighbors.heading: the boy who kept the name
neighbors.text: Today Bilal, under a rock in the sun, could only say: One, One. Hindus tell of a boy who held on like that. In the Bhagavata Purana, young Prahlada's father, a demon king, tries again and again to break his devotion to Vishnu. The boy is threatened and thrown into danger, and still he keeps remembering the Lord, until Vishnu himself comes to protect him.
neighbors.difference: Bilal's "One" refused every partner beside God. Prahlada's devotion is to Vishnu, whom he sees present everywhere, even in a pillar; and his rescue comes from Vishnu himself, while Bilal's came through a friend's money.
neighbors.shared: when you've almost no breath left, it can still hold what you love.

neighbors.heading: one, until the last breath
neighbors.text: Today one word was Bilal's whole answer: ahad, one. Jews say the sister of that word twice a day: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The Talmud tells how Rabbi Akiva, tortured by the Romans, recited it, and drew out the last word, echad, one, until his soul left him.
neighbors.difference: Bilal lived; Abu Bakr bought his freedom, and he became the voice of the call to prayer. Akiva died, and Jews remember him among martyrs who sanctified God's name. Each tradition prays its own words.
neighbors.shared: one word, said under pressure, can say everything you are.

neighbors.heading: the same Mary
neighbors.text: Today a Christian king wept to hear the Qur'an's chapter about Mary. Christians know her story from Luke: "And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." No wonder the court was moved. They heard someone they loved honored in another people's scripture.
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an honors Mary and the virgin birth, and Jesus as a prophet and servant of God. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God. The two books tell her story in their own ways.
neighbors.shared: it's moving to hear someone you love honored by a stranger.

neighbors.heading: a book with room
neighbors.text: Today a king heard holy words from another faith and recognized something true. Sikhs built that recognition into their scripture. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the hymns of the Sikh Gurus beside the verses of bhagats from other backgrounds, among them Kabir and the Muslim Sufi Sheikh Farid. Sikhs sing their words as gurbani, the Guru's word, and bow before them.
neighbors.difference: The Negus heard Christian figures told in the Qur'an's own words, then protected the people who recited them. The Guru Granth Sahib places other saints' words inside the Sikh scripture itself, to be sung as its own.
neighbors.shared: truth can sound like home even in a neighbor's voice.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, hymns of Sheikh Farid and Bhagat Kabir (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: they know not
neighbors.text: Today, offered revenge on the worst day of his life, the Prophet said no and hoped for his enemies' children instead. Catholics hear something close from the cross. Luke remembers Jesus, praying for the people who were killing him: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." The Church calls forgiving enemies a high point of Christian prayer.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet turned down the power to destroy and looked to the faith of generations not yet born. Jesus, Catholics believe, gave his life on that cross, and asked his Father to forgive the very people who put him there.
neighbors.shared: the hardest day can still end without a curse.
neighbors.sources: Luke 23:34 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2844 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: hatred doesn't end hatred
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet could have had the mountains close over Mecca, and refused. Buddhists have a verse for it. The Dhammapada, early in its first chapter, says: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." Answering hate with more hate only keeps it going.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet's mercy hoped that God would bring believers out of his enemies' line. The Dhammapada speaks of a law of the mind and heart, with no God sending angels or judging the outcome.
neighbors.shared: mercy on a bad day keeps a door open for people not yet born.

neighbors.heading: we will do
neighbors.text: Today twelve men promised a way of living: no stealing, no slander, no harming their children. Jews remember a people's promise at Sinai. When Moses read them the book of the covenant, they answered: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." The rabbis loved that they said "we will do" before anything else.
neighbors.difference: At Aqaba, twelve men pledged to the Prophet personally, and the reward was left with God. At Sinai, a whole people entered a covenant with God through Moses, which Jews understand as binding on their children ever after.
neighbors.shared: faith gets real in your hands, your tongue and your home.

neighbors.heading: be one
neighbors.text: Today's pledge wasn't about armies or money; it was about how to live, day to day. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, wrote himself a note in that spirit: "No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such." For the Stoics, a good life is something you practice, not just admire.
neighbors.difference: The twelve made their promise to a prophet, before God, and the hadith leaves room for God's forgiveness when they slip. Marcus wrote to himself; his reminder rests on reason and habit.
neighbors.shared: a good life is mostly small promises, kept.

neighbors.heading: why should I fear?
neighbors.text: Today, with searchers at the mouth of the cave, the Prophet asked: what of two, when God is their third? Sikhs sing a hymn of the same trust. Guru Arjan calls God father, mother, relative and brother, and says: when You are my protector everywhere, why should I fear or worry?
neighbors.difference: In the cave, God is the unseen third, close but beyond the two friends. In Sikh teaching, the one God is also the light within every heart, and the hymn speaks to God as family.
neighbors.shared: fear gets smaller when you know you aren't alone in it.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 103, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: do not grieve
neighbors.text: Today, in the cave, the Prophet told his friend: grieve not, God is with us. Near its close, the Bhagavad Gita has the same words. Krishna tells the frightened Arjuna to let go of every other support and take refuge in him alone: I will free you from every wrong; do not grieve.
neighbors.difference: In the cave, the words pass between two friends, and God is unseen. In the Gita, Krishna speaks them himself, face to face on a battlefield chariot, honored by many Hindus as God come to earth.
neighbors.shared: you can be careful and still let the fear go.

neighbors.heading: the bowl and the teaching
neighbors.text: Today the poorest believers lived on a bench inside the mosque, fed by gifts and listening close. Buddhist monks and nuns live by a similar trade. In many Buddhist lands they own almost nothing and eat what lay people put in their bowls, and the Buddha said the two help each other: the givers offer food and robes, and the monastics offer the teaching.
neighbors.difference: The people of the bench were poor because they had no family or wealth to fall back on, not by a vow. Buddhist monastics choose to give up possessions as part of their training.
neighbors.shared: the ones with the least can be the ones who remember the most.

neighbors.heading: all things common
neighbors.text: Today the poor were fed in the middle of the mosque, not at the edge of town. Christians remember the first church in Jerusalem doing something like it: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common; And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need."
neighbors.difference: In Medina, the Prophet sent charity to the bench and shared gifts with them. In Acts, the believers pooled what they owned, and Christians have lived that out in different ways since.
neighbors.shared: the people with the least belong in the middle of the room.

neighbors.heading: sing while you dig
neighbors.text: Today the whole city dug a trench, and the Prophet sang out a line while the diggers sang back. Psychologists have studied that. In one study by Oxford researchers, adults who joined a singing class felt close to each other faster than people who joined other group classes. Singing together seems to knit strangers into a team.
neighbors.difference: At the trench, the songs were prayers: asking God for forgiveness, calm and firm feet. The research measures the closeness people feel and doesn't ask who, if anyone, is listening.
neighbors.shared: hard work gets lighter when everyone sings the same line.
neighbors.sources: Pearce, Launay and Dunbar, "The ice-breaker effect," Royal Society Open Science, 2015 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the leader in the dirt
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet carried earth until the dust covered his belly. Catholics see their Lord kneel, too. At the Last Supper, Jesus washed his disciples' feet and said: "If then I being your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; you also ought to wash one another's feet." On Holy Thursday, many priests still kneel and wash people's feet.
neighbors.difference: At the trench, the Prophet worked beside everyone on a shared job. In John, Jesus does a servant's job for his disciples alone, and Catholics read it as a sign of the gift he gives on the cross.
neighbors.shared: the one in charge is not too big for the dirty work.

neighbors.heading: the right resolve
neighbors.text: Today Wahshi, Hind and Ikrimah, who had fought him, came back and found the door open. Hindus hear a door like that in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna says that even someone who has done great wrong, if they turn to him with an undivided heart, should be counted good, because they have made the right resolve.
neighbors.difference: The Prophet received the people who came to him, and the grief stayed real, as with Wahshi. In the Gita, Krishna speaks as the Lord himself, and the turning is devotion to him.
neighbors.shared: where you're headed can matter more than where you've been.

neighbors.heading: turn and live
neighbors.text: Today people who had done real harm walked back in, and weren't turned away. Jews call that turning teshuvah. God asks through the prophet Ezekiel: "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD; and not rather that he should return from his ways, and live?" The days before Yom Kippur are kept for that return.
neighbors.difference: In the stories, the Prophet welcomes people who come to him and to Islam. Jewish teshuvah is turning back to God, and for wrongs against a person, Jewish law asks you to make it right with them first.
neighbors.shared: the way back is there before you start walking it.

neighbors.heading: one blood
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet told a vast crowd that all people are children of Adam, and no color or nation is above another. Christians hear Paul in Athens say it too: God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Elsewhere Paul writes that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek.
neighbors.difference: In the sermon, the only measure of nobility is mindfulness of God. Paul goes on, in both places, to speak of Christ, and Christians hear the oneness of people fulfilled in him.
neighbors.shared: every face you meet comes from the same family.

neighbors.heading: one light
neighbors.text: Today: no Arab over a non-Arab, no light skin over dark. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps a hymn of Bhagat Kabir that even uses the name Allah. First God made the light, he sings; from that one light came everyone. So who is good, and who is bad? Sikhs see it in the langar, where all sit and eat in rows as equals.
neighbors.difference: The sermon names one measure of rank before God: mindfulness of Him. Kabir and the Sikh Gurus press hard against caste, and Sikhs teach that the same divine light shines in every person.
neighbors.shared: no one was made from a better batch of clay.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1349, Bhagat Kabir (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a cup of cold water
neighbors.text: Today Uthman bought a well and made its water free, his bucket beside everyone's. Catholics count "give drink to the thirsty" among the works of mercy, and Jesus said: "whosoever shall give to drink to one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward."
neighbors.difference: Uthman's well is sadaqah jariyah, flowing charity whose good keeps going after he dies. Jesus speaks of a single cup given in his name; Catholics see Christ himself in the one who receives it.
neighbors.shared: water given away keeps doing good long after the giving.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 10:42 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: goodness that grows
neighbors.text: Today a well became a gift that kept flowing. The Buddha said almost the same about wells. Asked whose merit keeps growing, he answered: those who plant groves and orchards, build bridges, give wells and places to drink, and shelter for travelers. Their goodness, he said, grows day and night.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, flowing charity carries its reward to the giver from God, even after death. In Buddhism, merit comes from the act itself and the giving heart, with no God keeping the account.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts keep working while you sleep.

neighbors.heading: she reaches out her hands
neighbors.text: Today the "longest hand" turned out to be the giving one: Zaynab worked with her hands and gave from it. On Friday nights, many Jewish homes sing of a woman like her, from Proverbs: she works wool and flax with her own hands, and "She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy."
neighbors.difference: Zaynab's riddle came true in one real woman Aisha remembered. The woman of valor in Proverbs is a portrait, sung at the Shabbat table to honor the women of the house.
neighbors.shared: the longest reach belongs to the hands that give.

neighbors.heading: giving feels better
neighbors.text: Today the wives measured their arms, and the answer was charity. Psychologists have measured something too. In a study by Elizabeth Dunn and colleagues, people handed a little money were happier by evening if told to spend it on someone else than if told to spend it on themselves. Giving seems to come back to the giver.
neighbors.difference: Zaynab gave for God, and the riddle pointed to her place beside the Prophet after death. The study measures one evening's happiness and makes no promise beyond it.
neighbors.shared: giving tends to fill the hands that give.
neighbors.sources: Dunn, Aknin and Norton, "Spending money on others promotes happiness," Science, 2008 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: remember, remember
neighbors.text: Today Fatimah, worn from the mill, was given words to repeat at night instead of a servant. Sikhs know that gift. The Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's long hymn of peace, opens by asking you to remember God, remember, and remember, and so find peace. Sikhs pair it with honest work: remember the Name, earn by your own labor, share what you have.
neighbors.difference: Fatimah's words are counted: praise, thanks and God's greatness, in set numbers, before sleep. Sikh simran centers on the Name, often Waheguru, repeated through the day, with no count required.
neighbors.shared: tired hands can still hold a few holy words.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the offering of repeating
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet gave his daughter words to count, better for her than a servant. Hindus count holy words too, often on a string of beads. It's called japa. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna lists the ways he shows himself in the world, and says that among all offerings, he is japa, the quiet repeating of a sacred name.
neighbors.difference: Fatimah's words praise the one God, counted at day's end. Japa is often a name of a deity, like Rama or Krishna, or the syllable Om, and many Hindus count it on beads at any hour.
neighbors.shared: a few words, repeated, can carry a long day.

neighbors.heading: water or blood?
neighbors.text: Today Hasan had an army like mountains, and chose a settlement instead. Buddhists tell of the Buddha stepping between two clans, his own Sakyans and the Koliyans, armed and ready to fight over a river's water. He asked them which was worth more, the water or the lives of the warriors. They put down their weapons.
neighbors.difference: Hasan gave up a claim to rule, and Sunni and Shia Muslims read his choice in different lights. The Buddha wasn't giving up anything of his own; he reasoned with both sides until they saw the cost.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the strongest move is the one that keeps everyone alive.

neighbors.heading: the peacemakers
neighbors.text: Today a grandson was named a peacemaker before he was grown, and became one. Christians hear Jesus say it on the mount: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Christians have long read it as an active calling: not only avoiding fights, but making peace between others.
neighbors.difference: Hasan's peace was a hard settlement between two armies, praised in a hadith. Jesus' blessing names peacemakers "children of God," which Christians hear as sharing the life of his Father.
neighbors.shared: making peace can take more strength than winning.

neighbors.heading: rich in what you let go
neighbors.text: Today a perfumed young man gave up everything, and left the world in a cloak too short to cover him. Henry David Thoreau, who went to live simply by a pond, wrote: "a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone." For Thoreau, freedom grew as wants grew smaller.
neighbors.difference: Mus'ab gave up comfort for his faith and died at Uhud for it. Thoreau's simplicity was an experiment in living, chosen for freedom and clear sight, without a promise of reward after death.
neighbors.shared: what you can let go of can't own you.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (Thoreau)

neighbors.heading: Francis gave back his clothes
neighbors.text: Today Mus'ab traded fine clothes for a patched cloak. Catholics love a young man who did that: Saint Francis of Assisi, a rich merchant's son, gave back even the clothes he wore to his father, in front of the bishop, to follow Christ in poverty. He was answering a call Jesus gave: "go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor."
neighbors.difference: Mus'ab was cut off by his family for his faith and kept nothing back. Francis chose poverty as a way of imitating Christ, and founded a brotherhood that still takes that vow.
neighbors.shared: the ones who gave the most up are remembered with the most love.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 19:21 (Douay-Rheims) · Bonaventure, Life of Saint Francis, ch. 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: four places to look
neighbors.text: Today Mu'adh gave his order: the book, then the Prophet's example, then careful reasoning. Hindus know a ladder like it. The Manusmriti names four marks of dharma, of what's right: the Veda, the remembered tradition, the conduct of good people, and, last, what satisfies your own inner self.
neighbors.difference: For Mu'adh, reason works inside the book and the sunnah, never against them. Hindu sources are many and its schools weigh them differently, and the inner self in the list is a conscience shaped by that tradition.
neighbors.shared: start with what's been handed down, then think hard and honestly.

neighbors.heading: it is not in heaven
neighbors.text: Today: the book first, then the sunnah, then your own careful reasoning. Jews read the Torah through the oral tradition and the arguments of rabbis. Moses tells Israel the commandment "is not in heaven." The Talmud tells of rabbis who quoted that line to keep deciding by reasoning and majority, even when a voice from heaven spoke up.
neighbors.difference: In the Mu'adh report, reasoning is the last step, when the book and sunnah are silent. Talmudic debate keeps minority opinions on the page and makes argument itself a holy study.
neighbors.shared: the old words are given to us to think with, not around.

neighbors.heading: the persecutor preaches
neighbors.text: Today the man whose horsemen broke the lines at Uhud became "the sword of God." Christians know a turn like that. Saul hunted the first Christians, until he met Jesus on the road to Damascus. Afterward the churches said in wonder: "he which persecuted us in times past now preacheth the faith which once he destroyed."
neighbors.difference: Khalid came to Medina, and the Prophet taught that Islam wipes out what came before it. For Christians, Paul's turn began with Jesus himself appearing to him, and Paul wrote that anyone in Christ is a new creature.
neighbors.shared: people change, and a community can make room for them.

neighbors.heading: Sajjan the thug
neighbors.text: Today an old enemy came in and became a defender. Sikhs tell of a man named Sajjan, whose name means friend. He welcomed travelers to his inn and then robbed and killed them. Guru Nanak stayed the night and sang a hymn about things that shine outside and are dark within. Sajjan fell at his feet, confessed, and began to serve travelers instead.
neighbors.difference: Khalid's past was in battle, and he turned when he came to Islam in Medina. Sajjan's story comes from the janamsakhis, the Sikh life stories of Guru Nanak, and his change came through one hymn and one night.
neighbors.shared: nobody's worst chapter has to be their last.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Guru Nanak and Sajjan (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: sick, and you visited me
neighbors.text: Today a woman kept a tent for the wounded, right in the mosque. Catholics count caring for the sick as a work of mercy, because Jesus said the one in need is him: "sick, and you visited me." That line helped inspire hospitals, and orders of sisters who gave their lives to nursing.
neighbors.difference: Rufaydah's tent stood beside the place of prayer, and she served wounded believers. Catholics hear Jesus saying that in caring for the sick, they care for Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: healing belongs right beside prayer, not behind it.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:36 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: tend the sick
neighbors.text: Today Rufaydah did the unglamorous part: wounds, water, care. Buddhists tell of the Buddha finding a monk lying sick in his own filth, with no one helping. He and Ananda washed him and laid him on a bed. Then he told the monks: whoever would care for me should care for the sick.
neighbors.difference: Rufaydah's care is remembered as service to God's people, close to the Prophet. The Buddha taught that monks have no mother or father to nurse them, so they must nurse each other; tending the sick is how they tend him.
neighbors.shared: the person no one is helping is the one to help first.

neighbors.heading: honor thy mother
neighbors.text: Today the one deed the Prophet named for Uways was his care for his mother. Jews hear the commandment at Sinai: "Honour thy father and thy mother." The Talmud tells of a gentile, Dama ben Netina, who passed up a huge sale rather than wake his sleeping father for the key. The rabbis held him up as the model.
neighbors.difference: For Uways, care for his mother is remembered as what kept him from ever meeting the Prophet. In the Torah, honoring parents is one of the Ten Commandments, with a promise of long days attached.
neighbors.shared: caring for a parent is holy work, even when no one sees it.

neighbors.heading: from my mother
neighbors.text: Today Uways stayed home for his mother, and was honored for it. Marcus Aurelius, ruler of an empire, began his private notebook by thanking the people who made him, and his mother is near the top: "From my mother, piety and beneficence." He goes on to thank her for teaching him to live simply.
neighbors.difference: Uways cared for his mother with his days, and the Prophet tied it to God's favor. Marcus wrote thanks for what she gave him, as part of a practice of seeing clearly where his good came from.
neighbors.shared: who we are started with someone who took care of us.

neighbors.heading: Guru and disciple
neighbors.text: Today a new leader said: I'm not the best of you; if I go wrong, set me right. Sikhs remember a leader who bowed like that. Sikh tradition says that after Guru Gobind Singh gave amrit to the first five of the Khalsa, he knelt and asked those five to give it to him too. Sikhs praise him as both Guru and disciple.
neighbors.difference: Abu Bakr was chosen by pledge and set obedience to God as the limit of his own. Guru Gobind Singh was the Guru himself, and in Sikh belief he later passed guidance to the scripture and the Khalsa together.
neighbors.shared: a good leader asks to be corrected, out loud.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of the first amrit (paraphrase) · Bhai Gurdas II, Var 41 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the people's good is the king's
neighbors.text: Today a leader said the weak would be strong in his eyes until he got them their right. Hindus know a ruler's duty like that, rajadharma. The Arthashastra, an old Indian manual on governing, says a king's happiness lies in his people's happiness, and his good in their good, not in what pleases him.
neighbors.difference: Abu Bakr invited the people to correct him and set God's command as the limit. The Arthashastra speaks to kings born to rule, and grounds their duty in dharma, not in the people's pledge.
neighbors.shared: power is a trust, and the weakest are the test of it.

neighbors.heading: not by birth
neighbors.text: Today a governor's son thought his father's name made him untouchable, and Umar answered: their mothers bore them free. The Buddha said something like it to a proud man who called him an outcast. Not by birth is anyone an outcast, he said, and not by birth is anyone a brahmin. By what you do, you become one or the other.
neighbors.difference: Umar's line rests on birth itself: everyone is born free, and justice must be evenhanded before God. The Buddha's point is that worth comes from your actions, not from family or caste.
neighbors.shared: nobody's name makes them more of a person than you.

neighbors.heading: no respect of persons
neighbors.text: Today a Christian from Egypt crossed a desert, and the caliph took his side over a governor's son. Christians have a letter that warns against just that kind of favoritism: "My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons." James goes on: don't seat the rich man well and the poor man on the floor.
neighbors.difference: In the story, a Muslim ruler judges by the Qur'an's call for evenhanded justice. James writes to Christians about their own gatherings, tying fairness to faith in Christ.
neighbors.shared: justice that bends for the powerful isn't justice.

neighbors.heading: Socrates stayed
neighbors.text: Today Uthman, surrounded, sent his defenders home rather than let blood be shed for him. Socrates faced a choice like that. Condemned to death in Athens, he was offered an escape his friend Crito had arranged. Socrates refused: he had lived under the city's laws all his life, and would not answer an unjust verdict with a wrong of his own.
neighbors.difference: Uthman read his choice through the Prophet's words about a trial and a shirt, and readers still argue about it. Socrates reasoned his way there in conversation, out of loyalty to justice and his city.
neighbors.shared: sometimes holding your ground means refusing to fight for yourself.

neighbors.heading: put up thy sword
neighbors.text: Today Uthman forbade anyone to fight for him. Catholics remember the night Jesus was arrested. A disciple drew a sword to defend him, and Jesus said: "Put up again thy sword into its place: for all that take the sword shall perish with the sword." Then he let himself be led away.
neighbors.difference: Uthman refused to let Muslims kill Muslims for his sake, and Muslims remember the years after as a time of strife. Catholics believe Jesus went freely to the cross to save the world.
neighbors.shared: refusing to shed blood for yourself is its own kind of courage.
